hmmt-feb-1998-team-01a.prompt:
A *graph* is a collection of points and lines (or curves), called *vertices* and *edges*, where each edge connects exactly two distinct vertices and any two vertices are connected by at most one edge. Two vertices are *adjacent* if they are connected by an edge. Graph $\mathcal G$ is *isomorphic* to $\mathcal H$ ($\mathcal G\cong\mathcal H$) if the vertices of $\mathcal G$ can be renamed with the names of the vertices of $\mathcal H$ so that both graphs have the same edges. Edge crossings in a drawing are not vertices (vertices are drawn as dots).

Which of the six figures (i)-(vi) shown are graphs? List the vertices and edges of each graph and explain why the others are not graphs.
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01a.answer: Graphs: (i) vertices A,B,C,D, edges AB, AC, AD, BD; (iii) vertices A,B,C, edges AB, BC, AC; (iv) vertices A,B,C,D,E, edges AB, AD, AE, BE, CD, CE. Not graphs: (ii) A and B are joined by two edges; (v) an edge from B ends at no vertex; (vi) E is joined to itself.

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-ii.prompt:
The *chromatic number* $\chi$ of a graph is the smallest number of colors with which its vertices can be colored so that adjacent vertices get different colors.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a planar graph with $\chi>5$ that has a vertex $V$ of degree at most $5$. Prove that removing $V$ (and all edges at $V$) gives a graph with fewer vertices which also has $\chi>5$. You may use the Jordan Curve Theorem: a closed loop that does not intersect itself divides the plane into an inside and an outside, and a continuous curve joining a point inside to one outside must cross the loop.
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-ii.answer: If $\mathcal G-V$ were 5-colorable, recolor along two-colored chains (Kempe chains) until the neighbours of $V$ use at most 4 colors; then $V$ can be colored too.
